source.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
source.authors: Curt Tigges; Michael Hanna; Qi-Nan Yu; Stella Biderman

page_placements.theme: Training decides which heads carry suppressive roles and how strongly

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figures are represented by extracted/flattened text rather than readable plotted values.
record.tranche_reason: Extends copy-suppression circuit analysis to Pythia models across training checkpoints and model scales, rather than testing GPT-2 small L10H7 with the original distribution-wide loss analysis.
record.gate_note: The study reports copy-suppression component scores in IOI circuits and path-patching results for IOI circuits. Figure 2 gives curves without extractable numeric values; the text says copy-suppression heads emerge on a similar timescale but with varying speeds and strengths. Figure 4B reports a combined Copy Suppression/Name Mover path-patching measure. These results do not test calibration or the 76.9% loss-effect claim. The paper's discussion of self-repair is confined to a local IOI-circuit observation, not a distribution-wide comparison of repair mechanisms.
record.test_reason: The study scores Pythia IOI-circuit heads (160m–2.8b) with the original paper's CSPA metric across 300B tokens of training. It reports copy-suppression heads in every analysed model, with a direction-of-effect result that differs from GPT-2 small. It also gives a qualitative self-repair observation for negative heads in Pythia-160m. This bears on V5 (other models and sizes, narrow-task negative heads) and V4. It never studies GPT-2 small L10H7, so V1 and V2 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. The authors conclude that task abilities and functional components (including copy-suppression heads) emerge at similar token counts across Pythia scales. They find that the IOI algorithm stays stable even as individual heads change roles, and that circuit size grows with model size. They add that Pythia copy-suppression heads help IOI by downweighting the incorrect name. Self-repair and load-balancing mechanisms are left to future work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the copy-suppression-preserving-ablation metric associated with the original work, but studies Pythia IOI-circuit heads across training and scale rather than GPT-2 small L10H7's effect on loss across the training distribution.
record.method_sensitivity: Copy-suppression component scores vary in emergence speed and strength across model sizes and checkpoints. The IOI circuit analysis also samples every checkpoint for Pythia-160m but approximately one third of available checkpoints for larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia-160m, individual heads gain and lose functional roles over training, including CS heads among the top-5 tracked, while other heads take over. The IOI algorithm-level metrics stay stable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The copy-suppression role in a circuit is not tied to a fixed head across training; it can migrate between heads while task performance is preserved.

record.peer_reviewed: Workshop on Representation Learning for NLP (2024); the paper text also carries a NeurIPS 2024 header.
record.problems: The copy-suppression score curves are figure-only in the supplied text, without extractable numeric values or uncertainty estimates. The IOI analysis covers a narrow task and one model family; it does not establish distribution-wide behavior. The self-repair observation is qualitative and localized.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant copy-suppression results were omitted. Other task curves and circuit-graph statistics were not included because they do not report outcomes specific to the claim's copy-suppression behavior or self-repair versions.

untested.parts: All of it: GPT-2 small L10H7 is not studied.
QK/OV weight circuits and the share of loss effect they explain.
Magnitude of compensation; settings beyond the Pythia-160m IOI circuit at 300B tokens.
Model families other than Pythia; tasks other than IOI; absolute CSPA magnitudes comparable to L10H7.
Relative share of copy suppression versus other self-repair sources.

missing.what: Pythia CS heads contribute positively to IOI by downweighting the incorrect (repeated subject) name, the opposite sign from GPT-2's IOI copy-suppression heads.
missing.locator: Section 3.2 (Copy Suppression Heads paragraph); Appendix D referenced

missing.what: Pythia-160m final IOI circuit lists separate positive CS (8.9), negative CS (9.5) and negative name-mover (9.1) heads.
CS heads (CSPA >10%) present among direct-effect heads in all models 160m–2.8b.
Per-head CSPA trajectories for Pythia-160m; the y-axis appears to span 0–0.006, which needs checking against the plot.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 links are wrong: no GPT-2 small analysis exists in this paper. Figure 2 normalisation makes the CSPA rows unreadable for strength. The ioi-csnm rows measure combined CS and name-mover heads and should not carry V5. The most informative V5 evidence (the direction of CS effect in IOI, and separate positive and negative CS heads) is in the text and Figure 4A, and no row records it.

versions.untested_parts: Does not identify or test GPT-2 small L10H7, establish one head's main role across the full training distribution, or compare that role against all other roles of a head on ordinary text.
Whether QK and OV weights explain most of a head's effect on loss, including the 76.9% figure.
Calibration and overconfidence in naive copying.
Whether copy suppression contributes substantially to self-repair across the training distribution or under other upstream-copier ablations.
Whether negative name movers in IOI or heads in other models and sizes beyond the tested Pythia suite implement the same role.
The relative prevalence or magnitude of copy suppression versus other self-repair mechanisms across the distribution.
